lessons.title: You Have to Demonstrate Loyalty to Receive It

items.paragraph: (Download the transcript below)

attachment.originalUrl: Lesson 9 You Have to Demonstrate Loyalty to Receive It.pdf

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph:
Ah, employee loyalty. A lost art, right? With employees changing jobs every few years, people being more transient in general, and an ever-changing workplace, it feels like the days of 20- or 30-year employees and the “company” man or woman are gone.

This feeling isn’t completely unfounded. According to Forbes, the average tenure for an employee in recent years is around 4.1 years, offset by the fact that nearly 38 percent of employees quit within the first year.1 And why not?, you might ask. People have more options. People have more needs. There are more industries and companies than ever to choose from, and they’re more diverse.

items.name: – Pat Summitt
items.paragraph: Loyalty is a selfless proposition. You won’t ever have it unless you are willing to give it away first.”

lessons.title: Knowledge Check

items.title: What is the average tenure for modern employees?

answers.title: 2 years
4 years
5 years
7 years

items.title: Which is not a contributing factor to employee turnover?

answers.title: People have more options to choose from than ever before.
Employees have a diversity of needs/requirements from an employer.
People don’t want to work hard.
All of the above are contributing factors.

items.title: Complete this statement (from Pat): “Loyalty is a selfless proposition. You won’t ever have it unless you___________.”

answers.title: Command it from those you lead.
Clarify exactly what is expected of the team.
Get the terms and conditions in writing.
Are willing to give it away first.

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph: The recent increase in employee turnover has led to a countering philosophy on the end of employers: Everyone is expendable. With full-time HR departments packed with recruiters, filling seats to replace empty ones has become a booming industry in itself. A new culture has emerged on behalf of the organization: Hire all the top talent you can find, and let nature take its course. We’ll do our best, but if people don’t like it, they can leave, and we’ll replace them with another highly paid person. No one’s really expecting team members to have loyalty, and the organization or company is not showing loyalty in return.

The kicker is… no one really likes this arrangement. Not the employee, not the employer. No matter how practical the hiring industry becomes, if you’re an employee, it can be exhausting to look for jobs every four years. If you’re an employer, it can cost up to 33 percent of an employee’s salary to replace the ones who leave ($15,000 for a $45,000 full-time position).2 Not to mention the impact it makes on an organization’s culture and employees’ sense of well-being.

On their end, employees have watched employers over-hire thousands of employees, then layoff thousands at a time to balance things out when the market corrects. Employees who do survive the layoffs often end up watching their colleagues being axed through emails with little notice, and are then asked to plod on, showing unquestioning loyalty to the company. Employers, by contrast, have scrambled to implement the best benefits programs and most flexible work arrangements available, only to watch their employee base hemorrhage through mass exoduses.

items.name: — Pat Summitt
items.paragraph: If you want to develop loyalty, the first thing you have to do is demonstrate it. Too many people use the term loyalty unilaterally. Especially bosses. They demand loyalty without reciprocating. They ask ‘Staff, have you been loyal to me?’ But what about the manager’s loyalty to the staff?”

lessons.title: You Win in Life With People

items.paragraph:
Pat believed the single most common reason organizations self-destruct is disloyalty.

When asked about her championship teams, she famously said, “If you want to demonstrate loyalty, the first thing you have to do is demonstrate it. Too many people use the term loyalty unilaterally. Especially bosses. They demand loyalty without reciprocating. They ask ‘Staff, have you been loyal to me?’ But what about the manager’s loyalty to the staff?”3

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph: In the upcoming lessons we’ll learn more on how to be loyal to your team, and how to be a leader no one will ever want to leave.

items.name: — Pat Summitt
items.paragraph: You win with people. I don’t care how good you are. I don’t care what kind of genius you may be. If you don’t have a good, loyal staff, you will not succeed.”
